edges.effect_quant: In premature coronary disease, visceral adipose tissue in the highest tertile (at least 194 cm²) was associated with a 2.71-fold higher recurrent-MACE risk over 5 years. In 33,432 UK Biobank participants, elevated visceral-fat proportion remained associated with MACE after adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, with adjusted hazard ratios around 1.37 in females and 1.22 in males. A second UK Biobank body-composition analysis found higher VAT index associated with higher ASCVD risk (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.23).
edges.population: middle-aged and older adults with imaging-derived body composition assessment, including primary-prevention populations and people with established premature coronary disease
edges.mechanism: Visceral adipose tissue is metabolically active and drains into portal and systemic pathways that promote insulin resistance, inflammatory signaling, dyslipidemia, and endothelial dysfunction. Those processes help explain why visceral fat often carries more event risk than body mass index alone.
edges.summary: The strongest claim is that high visceral adipose tissue is a harmful cardiovascular-risk phenotype, especially when measured directly by imaging rather than inferred from BMI alone. Across contemporary cohorts, people with more visceral fat generally show more future major cardiovascular events, even after basic anthropometric adjustment.
edges.caveats: The size of the risk signal varies by population and by whether models adjust for other body-composition compartments. Some studies suggest low skeletal muscle or fat infiltration adds prognostic information alongside visceral fat, so this edge should be read as part of a broader body-composition risk pattern rather than as a stand-alone determinant.
